before: From Timothy: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the command of God our Savior, to Timothy, my true child in faith.” (1 Timothy 1:1) The name Savior fits no one else properly and truly — except the one who is God by nature. So the mystagogue has named him that even here. Yet our Lord Jesus Christ is also Savior: he is named Jesus, and the blessed angel made the force of the name clear: “You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” (Matthew 1:21) So Christ is God, if he is Savior of all people, as the inspired Paul says.

From Titus: “For the saving grace of God has appeared to all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires and to live soberly, justly, and godly in the present age, awaiting the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works.” (1 Timothy 4:10)

What grace has appeared to us, or of what God — though it is called saving for all people? Clearly “the Lord, being God, has also appeared to us,” (Titus 2:11–14) as blessed David says. We await his appearing of glory from the heavens. And he himself is our great God and Savior, Jesus the Christ, who has given himself for us so that, freeing us from all sin, he may present to himself genuine worshipers (Psalm 118:27).

before: “For it is not angels he takes hold of, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in things toward God, to make propitiation for the people’s sins. For in that he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.” (Hebrews 2:16–18)

We say the Word of God takes hold of Abraham’s seed: for he sprang from Judah according to the flesh, and was made like his brothers in every respect — at least in consenting to take the form of a slave (Philippians 2:7) and to come to be in the likeness of humans, as blessed Paul says. So he has been called Son of Man, and has become brother to those of Abraham’s seed… “so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest.” Merciful, because the letter of the law condemns sinners… yet Christ justifies by faith… Faithful, because he is lasting, continuous, and worthy of trust for what was promised.

“In that he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.” For he endured under temptation and endured the cross. Yet the Son has offered himself as a spotless victim to God the Father, so that through his own flesh he might help those who labor (Hebrews 7:23–25)… “For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified.” (Hebrews 10:14) So he himself has become high priest according to the human, though divinely he receives the sacrifices from all; himself the victim according to the flesh; himself the one who propitiates for our sins, according to the authority of the deity. So there is one Lord Jesus Christ.

before: A stone of stumbling and a rock of offense (Romans 9:33); and the one who believes upon him will not be put to shame. When righteous Symeon received the divine infant into his arms, he said to God: “Now you release your servant, Master, according to your word in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation which you prepared before the face of all the peoples,” (Luke 2:29–34) and what follows; and he added: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign spoken against.” (Isaiah 28:16) So the same one is the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense; and some, striking against him through disobedience, were shattered, while those who received the faith toward him escaped being put to shame. Have we then believed as toward a human, or as toward God? Clearly as toward God. Therefore Christ is God; for it was upon him that righteous Symeon spoke the words just now cited to us.

Concerning the Jews he says: “For not knowing the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they were not subjected to the righteousness of God; for Christ is the end of the law unto righteousness to everyone who believes.” (Romans 10:3–9) If Christ is the end of the law, and he himself is the righteousness who justifies through the faith toward him, and the power to justify belongs to God alone as his own, how is Christ not God?

“But the righteousness from faith says thus: Do not say in your heart, Who will ascend into heaven?—that is, to bring Christ down—or, Who will descend into the abyss?—that is, to bring Christ up from the dead (Romans 10:6–7). But what does it say? The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart—that is, the word of faith which we proclaim: that if you confess with your mouth Jesus as Lord,”

before: From Luke. “And it came to pass while they were there that the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her son, the firstborn, and wrapped him and laid him in the manger, because there was no place for them in the lodging.” (Luke 2:6–7) The holy virgin has borne one and only son, Emmanuel. How then does it say “her son, the firstborn” (Romans 8:29)? For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin. So it is marked from the God-breathed scripture: the Only-begotten Word of God has been named firstborn. For he has shared blood and flesh and similarly to us shared the same things. Thus he became firstborn among many brothers; yet as God he is worshiped by us ourselves and by the spirits above.

“And his mother said to him: Child, why have you done thus to us? See, your father and I, being in pain, were seeking you. And he said to them: Why is it that you were seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things of my Father?” (Luke 2:48–49) Observe how he names as his own Father the one in the heavens. But if he were a human alone, and understood as that very thing according to us, how would it not rather have been necessary to say: Did you not know that I must be in the things of the Father of all? But he makes him his own. For he alone has been begotten from him by nature divinely; and the same one, having also become human, has God as Father by nature and as his own.
